### Beijing Confirms the Three Presidents for Thursday in Shenzhen, the Airlines Open Monday With 55 Flights Cancelled Against the Fully-Normal Promise, and Asia Sells the Chip Stocks Ahead of Nvidia's Report While Alaska's Count Still Waits

Filed as: Edition No. 54 — The Overnight Watch · 2026-11-16T04:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-16-overnight-watch.html

The Night File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Beijing Confirms the Three Presidents for Thursday in Shenzhen, the Airlines Open Monday With 55 Flights Cancelled Against the Fully-Normal Promise, and Asia Sells the Chip Stocks Ahead of Nvidia’s Report While Alaska’s Count Still Waits

 The night file: the host’s confirmation completes the Shenzhen meeting from all three sides; a recovery morning counted at 55 cancellations before it begins; a third carrier in the Gulf and a gas field struck in Iraq; a Senate count that spent the night where Saturday left it; a petition past 160,000 in one account with the board still silent; and an Asian session that sold the chipmakers from Taipei to Seoul.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Monday, November 16, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 53, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, from Edition No. 52, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Sunday, from Edition No. 50, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Sunday, and from Edition No. 49, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Sunday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the overnight figures differ from the earlier figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Night in Brief: A Meeting Completed, a Recovery Opened, and No Count Moved

The night completed one meeting, opened one recovery, and moved no count. Beijing’s confirmation, carried in the confirmation account filed below, makes the Shenzhen session of Thursday official from all three capitals, two days after the White House announced it and one after the Kremlin confirmed it. The airlines’ Monday stands at 55 flights cancelled as of Sunday evening in the wire account filed below, the smallest opening figure of the four days, against the Secretary’s promise that the system would be probably fully normal on Monday. The Gulf gained a third American carrier and a struck gas field in Iraq and no word on the radar at Al-Riffa. Alaska’s count did not move in the night; its next count is due today. The petition for Mr. Huang passed 160,000 signatures in the Seoul account filed below, and the board’s answer is still not in the file. Asia opened the week by selling the chip stocks, Taiwan’s index closing down 6.0 percent in the closing account filed below. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the night settled is short: the meeting is confirmed, Monday’s cancellations are counted in the dozens and not the thousands, and every dated thing on the calendar—Mr. Warsh at noon, the count in Juneau, the President’s departure—still stands where Sunday left it. What it left open is the rest of the file: the root cause, the radar, the call, and the board.

The Airlines at 0400: Monday Opens at 55 Cancelled, Sunday’s Finals Stand Apart, and the Itemized Request Is Due Today

Monday opens with the smallest number of the four days, and the desk prints the three counts of it that the night carried. As of Sunday evening, 55 flights within, into or out of the United States scheduled for Monday were cancelled, in the wire account above; an earlier Sunday-afternoon count put Monday’s cancellations at 144, in the timeline account filed below; and the tracker account filed with the midnight edition counted 33 on Sunday afternoon. The three readings were taken at different hours of the same afternoon and evening, and they agree on the order of the day: a normal Monday schedule carries cancellations in the dozens, and Sunday closed in the thousands.

Sunday’s own final figures stand apart in the same file and are printed in the cocked hat: more than 2,300 cancelled in the Reuters count carried at midnight, more than 1,960 in the wire account above, and 18,689 delays in the timeline account against some 7,700 in the wire’s. No second stop was ordered in the night, and no Administration statement after the Secretary’s Sunday programmes stands in the overnight file.

The cause file gained two sentences and no answer. Two people familiar with the investigation said the router installation itself went smoothly, and that a detailed procedure of each step of the process is submitted to the Administration, in the Reuters account filed below. Both routers are with L3Harris, the contractor that owns and operates the network, while Administration staff are on site and the Federal Bureau of Investigation is offering support, in the El Dorado account filed below; the contractor said in a statement on Saturday that it was cooperating with the review and took the stop’s impact on travellers, airlines and operations seriously, in the same account’s file. The money file waits on Monday: the Secretary said a full, itemized request would be detailed Monday, in the Washington reporting carried in the El Dorado account; his Thursday letter to lawmakers asked for $30.1 billion, in the same account, against the $50 billion he has sought since Friday and the $12.5 billion approved last year, of which two House members say about $11 billion remains unspent. Settled: Monday’s opening count. Open: the root cause, in the Secretary’s own Sunday words, and the itemized request.

The Gulf at 0400: A Third Carrier in the Region, ‘Highly Unlikely’ From the President, a State of War From Tehran, and a Gas Field Struck in Iraq

The Gulf’s night was naval and verbal. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group entered the Central Command area on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington in the Arabian Sea—three carriers in the region, in a force of more than 20 ships enforcing the blockade of Iranian ports—in the carrier account filed below, which records that the presence is expected to be temporary as strike groups rotate and that all three could stay if necessary.

The words matched the deployment in both directions. The President told reporters on Sunday that new strikes on Iran are ‘highly unlikely’ as long as negotiations keep making progress, and that the United States could hit Iran’s nuclear facilities ‘within five minutes’ if needed, in the same account. Tehran’s deputy foreign minister, Mr. Gharibabadi, said in a televised interview that Iran is preparing for three scenarios—diplomacy, economic blockade and military aggression—and that ‘from a legal perspective, we are still in a state of war,’ in the same account; his list of demands stands there whole: a permanent end to the war on all fronts, removal of the blockade, the frozen assets resolved, and sanctions lifted, including on oil. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf said the conflict could end if Washington accepted Iran’s ‘logical conditions’ and warned that if the United States resumes strikes, Iran’s forces would ‘determine the geography of battle,’ in the same account.

Two claims in the file gained no assessment in the night. On the radar at Al-Riffa, the file stands where midnight left it: six drones in the Guards’ account, intercepts in Manama’s, no impacts to American forces in the Central Command spokesman’s sentence, and no word from any capital on the radar itself. In Iraq, a drone struck the Khor Mor gas field in Sulaymaniyah province on Sunday, setting off a large fire and cutting nearly 2,800 megawatts of regional generation; no group has claimed it, Kurdish officials called it a terrorist attack, and the Iraqi prime minister’s office ordered a joint investigation with the Kurdish authorities, in the carrier account. In Hormuz, the Guards’ claim that two tankers struck mines and that a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels sank stands unconfirmed in every account; a British monitor cited a report from Indian shipping authorities of a tanker attacked in the Gulf on November 15, its crew safe and accounted for, with no details of damage, in the maritime account filed below—an attack confirmed, a sinking not.

One Washington paper joined the file in the night. An Army major who survived the March 1 drone attack on the Port Shuaiba command post in Kuwait, which killed six American soldiers, filed a whistleblower complaint with the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Friday alleging that senior Army officials ignored warnings and failed to plan for anti-drone defences, in the carrier account; the Secretary of Defense said the day after that attack that the troops there were well protected, in the same account. The allegations are one officer’s, and no finding stands in the file.

Shenzhen at 0400: The Host Confirms, the Agendas Still Differ, and the Road Runs Through Manila

The meeting is now confirmed from all three sides, and the night’s largest fact is a confirmation. China’s Foreign Ministry said on Monday that President Xi will host a meeting of the heads of state of China, Russia and the United States in Shenzhen on Thursday, November 19, in the confirmation account above. The White House announced the plan on Friday through a communications official, Ms. Wales; the Kremlin confirmed on Saturday that the three countries had agreed to hold the summit; Beijing had said only that it was in communication with the relevant parties until Monday’s statement, in the same account.

The agendas still do not match, and the desk prints them side by side. Washington’s stated agenda starts with controlling and reducing nuclear arsenals and takes in the war in Iran; a senior American official told the Press the session is meant to begin a conversation on nuclear disarmament, with no agreement expected, in the confirmation account. The same official said Ukraine will not be discussed at the three-way session; the Kremlin aide, Mr. Ushakov, said on November 12 that the Ukraine settlement would be discussed with the President in Shenzhen, in the same account. No separate meeting between the President and President Putin is planned, in the same account; bilateral talks and a working lunch with President Xi stand on Thursday ahead of the three-way session.

The road to the room runs through Manila, and it begins today. The President is scheduled to leave Washington on Monday, attend the ASEAN summit in the Philippines on November 17, and travel to Shenzhen for the APEC leaders’ meeting of November 18 and 19, which President Xi chairs, in the confirmation account and in the itinerary account filed below. In Manila he will meet the leaders of India, Japan and Australia in a Quad summit on Tuesday, sign a trade deal with Thailand, and receive a state visit welcome on Wednesday, in the itinerary account. One American account notes what will travel with him: the matter of Mr. Huang’s chips will loom over the visit to Shenzhen, and American officials have said the President does not intend to raise the spying matter with President Xi, in the trip account filed below. Before he leaves, the President is scheduled to meet Qatar’s prime minister in Washington on Monday, in the carrier account filed above; Qatar has been stepping up its efforts to broker an end to the war.

Europe at 0400: A Channel Opened From Washington, No Call From Brussels, and Two Sentences From Moscow Unamended

Europe’s file gained a channel and no call. Mr. Kushner said in a social media post over the weekend that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand participation in the next round of talks to include European partners, in the force account filed below; an American account of the channel describes the focus of the diplomacy now as bringing Moscow and Europe into direct engagement and preparing the agenda for the next round of the trilateral talks, in the channel account filed below. No date, venue or format for direct Europe-to-Russia talks has been announced, in the same account.

Moscow’s two Sunday sentences stand unamended at 0400. The negotiators Europe has chosen have not yet attempted to make contact with Russia, the spokesman told the TASS agency, in the force account; and in the interview with a Vesti correspondent he said the settlement in Ukraine will be linked to a new security architecture on the European continent—‘two component parts, and neither can exist without the other’—and that absent a negotiated solution Russia will have to achieve its objectives by force, in the same accounts. Europe’s stated position, from the Council President, Mr. Costa, is that only Ukraine has the legitimacy to decide on matters concerning its territory and sovereignty, in the channel account. The next fact in this file is a telephone call that has not been made.

The Count at 0400: No Night Count, One Count Read Two Ways, and Monday as the Next Fact Again

Alaska’s count spent the night exactly where Saturday afternoon left it, and the overnight file adds an explanation and a spokesman, not a number. The state’s unofficial summary of Saturday at 1515 stands: Ms. Peltola 140,637 votes, 49.94 percent; Senator Sullivan 129,424, 45.96 percent; a lead of 11,213 on 281,587 votes in the race, in the state’s report filed with the midnight edition. The next count is due Monday, and at 0400 Eastern—midnight in Juneau—it had not been published in any account the desk read.

The two percentages that have followed this count for two days are one count read two ways, and an explainer in the night’s file sets the arithmetic out whole. The full summary counts the 872 write-in votes as cast, and 140,637 of 281,587 is 49.94 percent; the state’s dashboard excludes the unresolved write-ins from its display calculation, and 140,637 of 280,715 is 50.1 percent, in the explainer account filed below, which was checked on Monday, November 16, and which puts Ms. Peltola 157 votes short of a majority on the full denominator. Senator Sullivan’s spokesman, Mr. Adams, said the campaign was ‘still waiting for every ballot to be counted,’ in the count account filed below. Counting continues through Wednesday, November 18, the last day for overseas ballots and the day of the ranked-choice tabulation if no candidate holds a majority; certification is targeted for November 25. A victory for Ms. Peltola would give the Democrats a 56-to-44 Senate majority from January, in the count account. Settled: the arithmetic. Open: the call, which no desk has made.

Nvidia at 0400: A Petition Past 160,000 in One Account, a Shortlist Denied in Another, and No Answer From the Board

The petition passed another round number in the night, and the board passed another night in silence. More than 160,000 people have signed the petition for Mr. Huang’s reinstatement, in the Seoul account above; an open letter in the same file passed 157,000 signatures by Sunday, in the letter account filed below; and the petition account filed at midnight stood at 154,678 at 1001 Pacific on Sunday. The names behind the campaign are now listed in the open in the Seoul account: Mr. Musk, Mr. Sweeney of Epic Games, Mr. Tan of Y Combinator and Mr. Gomez of Cohere have publicly backed it, beside the investors Mr. Gerstner and Mr. Baker, whose letter asks the board to keep Mr. Huang’s return among the options in a slow and deliberate search.

One fact in the succession file moved against another. The board has denied reports that it shortlisted the chief of Arm, Mr. Haas, as a potential successor, in the letter account; the contest account filed at midnight recorded that the board has contacted the chief of Arm and states that no formal process has yet been initiated. Both sentences stand in the file, and the desk prints both. The Treasury Secretary’s Sunday position stands unamended: an outside successor, sweeping change, and answers from the board and external counsel within 10 days. The board itself had filed no public answer by 0400—to the petition, to the letter, or to the Treasury—in any account the desk read.

The interim file gained one number in the night. The interim chief, Ms. Kress, has cut the data centre guarantee to OpenAI from $250 billion to about $105 billion, in the morning account filed below, which puts the week’s focus on whether the company’s forward guidance is trimmed at Tuesday’s report; the company’s commitments and guarantees are separately reported in the market file to have jumped from $184 billion to more than $500 billion in one quarter. Earnings stand on Tuesday after the close: consensus revenue at $108.7 billion in the morning account, $108.9 billion in the week’s file, and $108.93 billion in the comeback account filed below. The stock fell 2.0 percent on Friday and about 13 percent on the week, in the morning account, and its market value has slipped below $4 trillion for the first time since July, in the comeback account. No finding has been made by the board, by any committee or by any court on any allegation in this file.

The Markets at 0400: Asia Sells the Chip Stocks, Japan Contracts, China Misses, and Mr. Warsh at Noon Is the Day’s Fact

Asia opened the week by selling the chip stocks, and the selling had a shape: it followed the Nvidia file and two sets of weak figures. Taiwan’s Taiex closed 6.0 percent lower and South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.6 percent, in the closing account above; an earlier account put the Kospi down about 2.6 percent in the session, with SK Hynix down over 6 percent and Samsung Electronics down 4 percent, in the morning wrap filed below. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 1.94 percent to about 59,780 in the morning wrap, on the day Japan’s economy was reported to have contracted 0.1 percent annualized in the third quarter against a consensus of growth, and China’s October figures missed their forecasts—retail sales up 0.4 percent against 0.8 expected, industrial output up 4.8 against 5.3—in the same account. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng held modest gains, up 0.25 percent in the wrap and 0.7 percent in the second morning account in the overnight file.

The American readings at 0400 are Sunday night’s, carried forward. Futures that opened higher at 1800 on Sunday stood lower by 2036—S&P 500 futures down 0.22 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures down 0.58, in the midnight file—and the morning accounts put them in the same place: S&P futures down about 0.2 percent and Nasdaq futures off roughly 0.5 percent, in the Asia account in the overnight file. Brent crude stood near $95.40 and West Texas crude near $87.10 in the same account, against $96.00 and $88.86 in the morning wrap; the oil market showed little reaction to the unconfirmed tanker claims, with a surplus forecast on the other side of the scale, in the wrap. Gold eased to about $3,873 an ounce and silver fell more than 3 percent, in the Asia account; gold fell 1.0 percent to $3,846 in the closing account. Bitcoin traded near $64,400 early Monday in the futures account filed below, at $64,641 in the closing account, and near $64,860 at 0040 Eastern in the overnight brief in the file—above the weekend’s low near $62,000 in every reading, and below Friday’s close in most.

The day’s market fact is scheduled, not traded: the central bank chairman, Mr. Warsh, opens a conference on artificial intelligence and productivity at noon Eastern, with the ten-year yield at 5.14 to 5.15 percent and the weekend’s officials—Mr. Schmid, Ms. Collins and Mr. Jefferson—all putting inflation at the centre of policy, in the Asia account. Tuesday carries retail sales and Nvidia; Wednesday, the October meeting minutes; Thursday, a listing in New York and Shenzhen.

France and Spain at 0400: A Fifth Day Counted in Custody Figures, and a Fourth Tracking That Moves Toward the Socialists

France’s file is a calendar with one new set of figures. Saturday’s fifth day of protest stands at 106,000 nationwide in the Interior Ministry’s count and about 200,000 in the organisers’; the night’s fullest account adds the policing figures—about 400 people stopped nationwide, 126 of them in Paris, and 108 held in custody in the capital, 38 of them minors, with some 70,000 police and gendarmes deployed—in the fifth-day account filed below, which records the police unions’ warning of fatigue after repeated weekend deployments. Tuesday’s strike stands, called by the unions after the rejection of the government’s 0.6 percent minimum-wage promise; Tuesday is the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement. The police bill—a presumption of legitimate self-defence for an officer who fires, a licence to kill in its critics’ phrase in the accounts—goes to the Senate on Thursday, November 19.

Spain’s campaign gained a fourth daily reading, and it moved toward the Socialists without moving the majority. The fourth instalment of the daily tracking puts the Popular Party at 31.5 percent, the Socialists at 30.3—past 30 percent for the first time and their best figure since the 2023 election—and Vox at 18.0, with the two right parties’ combined seats still above 190 against 176 needed, in the tracking account filed below. The third instalment, in the file, put the Popular Party at 31.4 percent and 128 seats, the Socialists at 29.9 and 119, and Vox at 18.3 and 62. The Sondaxe reading filed at midnight stands apart from both: Popular Party 30.8 and 130 seats, Socialists 26.4 and 106, Vox 18.2 and 65. The head-to-head debate between Mr. S&aacute;nchez and Mr. Feij&oacute;o stands on Thursday, November 19; polls may publish until November 23; Spain votes on November 29.

Monday Opens: Four Dated Tests and One Departure

Monday carries four dated tests and one departure. The airlines will be read against the Secretary’s fully-normal promise and an opening count of 55. Alaska’s count resumes ahead of Wednesday’s tabulation. Mr. Warsh speaks at noon. The President meets Qatar’s prime minister in Washington and then departs for Manila. Tuesday carries retail sales, France’s strike and Nvidia’s earnings after the close. Wednesday carries the October meeting minutes, the first day of APEC in Shenzhen and Alaska’s tabulation. Thursday carries the three presidents in Shenzhen, the Senate’s examination of the police bill in Paris, Spain’s debate and a listing in New York. The Treasury Secretary’s 10 days run from Sunday. Spain votes November 29; the Federal Reserve decides December 8 and 9. The Midday Watch collects at 1200.

The Cocked Hat

Where the night’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Monday’s flights: 55 cancelled as of Sunday evening in the wire’s account, 144 as of Sunday afternoon in the timeline account, and 33 on Sunday afternoon in the tracker account filed at midnight—three readings at three hours, agreeing that the day opens in the dozens. On Sunday’s cost: more than 2,300 cancelled in the Reuters count, more than 1,960 in the wire account, 1,606 at 1100 in the El Dorado account, and 18,689 delays in the timeline account against some 7,700 in the wire’s. On the router: an installation that went smoothly, in the words of two people familiar with the investigation, against a root cause still unknown in the Secretary’s. On the Gulf: three carriers and a blockade in the American account, a state of war in Tehran’s, new strikes highly unlikely in the President’s, and no word from any capital on the radar at Al-Riffa. On Hormuz: a supertanker sunk in the Guards’ claim, a tanker attacked with its crew safe in the monitor’s, and no vessel named in either. On Shenzhen: confirmed by all three capitals, with Ukraine on the agenda in the Kremlin aide’s telling and off it in Washington’s. On Europe: a channel opened from Washington, no call from Brussels, and objectives by force in Moscow’s interview. On Alaska: 49.94 percent on the full denominator, 50.1 on the dashboard, a victory declared by one candidate, every ballot awaited by the other, and no count in the night. On Nvidia: more than 160,000 signatures in the Seoul account, 157,000 in the letter account, 154,678 at midnight, a shortlist denied in one account and a contact reported in another, and no answer from the board. On Asia: the Kospi down 3.6 percent at the close in one account and 2.6 in the session in another; Brent at $95.40, $96.00 and $96.29 in three morning readings. On Spain: the Socialists at 30.3 percent in the fourth daily tracking and 26.4 in the Sondaxe reading, first in neither, with the right’s majority standing in both. Inside the triangle is where the week honestly opens, and the log turns on it.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 29 items.

 

 SubjectiveThe wire account — a return to normal expected on Monday, and 55 of Monday’s flights cancelled as of Sunday eveningUnited States air travel was expected to return to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following the no-takeoff order issued on Friday. As of Sunday evening, more than 55 flights within, into or out of the United States scheduled for Monday were cancelled, according to the tracker FlightAware, a dramatic shift from the more than 1,960 flights cancelled on Sunday in the same account. The ground stop issued on Friday afternoon was only the second such nationwide directive since the September 11 attacks and was blamed on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables. The Administrator had said on Saturday that travel would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday; the Secretary said on Sunday morning it would take longer to get planes, crews and travellers where they need to be, and that the system would be probably fully normal on Monday.

 SubjectiveThe timeline account — 9,000 cancelled on Friday, 144 of Monday’s down as of Sunday afternoon, and the routers at El Dorado and AmarilloThe Administration grounded departing flights at every United States airport on Friday, November 13, from 3:54 p.m. Eastern, with about 3,500 aircraft in the air, until the stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. About 9,000 flights were cancelled on Friday, roughly 6,400 more on Saturday, and cancellations carried into Sunday, when about 2,300 flights were cancelled and 18,689 delayed, according to FlightAware. Officials say the cause was network equipment, not a cyberattack: routers at Administration sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and Amarillo, Texas, flooded air traffic control systems with data during a copper-to-fiber upgrade, and the root cause is still being investigated. The Administrator says there is zero evidence of anything nefarious. Cancellations for Monday fell sharply, with 144 reported as of Sunday afternoon, and airlines expect near-normal operations on Monday with occasional knock-on cancellations possible.

 SubjectiveThe Apex Wire — 55 of Monday’s flights pre-cancelled, three days past 18,000, and the Administration’s Friday figure of 12,462United States air travel returns to normal on Monday after three days of disruption, with only about 55 Monday flights cancelled after more than 18,000 cancellations across the three days. The Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop at about 8:30 p.m. Eastern on Friday, ending a halt of about four and a half hours; more than 25,000 flights were delayed by 9:30 p.m. Friday, according to FlightAware. More than 6,150 flights were cancelled on Saturday and more than 7,300 delayed; Sunday brought more than 2,300 cancellations and about 7,700 delays, taking the three-day total past 18,000. The Administration later said operators cancelled about 12,462 flights on Friday, including 9,082 by major airlines, though not all were directly caused by the ground stop, and 827 flights were diverted. The stop was ordered after a telecommunications outage struck the air traffic control system, affecting all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

 SubjectiveReuters — more than 11,500 flights affected on Sunday, the installation went smoothly in two accounts, and the $50 billion requestUnited States air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 11,500 flights affected on Sunday, but the Transportation Secretary predicted a return to normalcy by Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following the systemwide ground stop. The Secretary said on a Sunday programme that there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other malicious intent, but the cause remained unclear, and that flights would come back to normal on Sunday but probably fully normal on Monday. The installation by the contractor L3Harris of at least one new router at a remote facility led to a situation in which other centers were overloaded with a flood of data; the replacement of a router at El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered problems with a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other centers. The functionality of the originating routers has been disabled, as was done for about 60 similar routers. The routers were purchased in 2001 and were obsolete by 2006. Two people familiar with the investigation said the router installation itself went smoothly, and that a detailed procedure of each step of the process is submitted to the Administration. The Secretary has called since Friday for $50 billion to upgrade the systems, up from $30 billion, after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year; two House members answered that about $11 billion of that sum remains unspent.

 SubjectiveSourceFirst News — both routers with L3Harris, the Bureau offering support, and a Thursday letter that asked for $30.1 billionFriday’s nationwide ground stop began when a newly installed router at a remote Administration site in El Dorado, Arkansas, started flooding the air traffic control network, the Transportation Secretary said on Sunday; officials still do not know whether the fault lay with the equipment or with the contractor that installed it. The Secretary said a second problem turned up at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where work had been done weeks earlier. Both routers are now with L3Harris, the contractor that owns and operates the network, while Administration staff are on site and the Federal Bureau of Investigation is offering support. Investigators are checking whether L3Harris installed the router wrongly or the device itself was faulty, and why the Amarillo site also started causing problems. The contractor owns the network that links the control facilities with remote radar sites and weather stations for voice and data. The Administrator said router swaps of this kind are routine and are not part of the $12.5 billion modernization effort Congress funded last year. The Secretary wants $50 billion in all and says last year’s money covers radar, radios and control centers but not telecom or software; a letter he and the budget director sent lawmakers on Thursday asked for $30.1 billion. The President broke his silence on the ground stop on Sunday by blaming the prior administration and urging Congress to pay for upgrading air traffic control. A governor said on Saturday that the Secretary must resign or be removed and called for a congressional investigation.

 SubjectiveThe carrier account — a third carrier enters the region, new strikes ‘highly unlikely,’ Tehran still at war, and a drone at Khor MorThe USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group entered the Central Command area of operations on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington, both already operating in the Arabian Sea, in a force of more than 20 Navy ships enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports; an American official said the three-carrier presence is expected to be temporary as strike groups rotate, though all three could stay if necessary. The Guards said they launched six drones at an American air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain on Sunday, describing the strike as a response to American aggression and claiming a successful impact; Bahrain’s military said it intercepted the attacks before they hit their targets. The President told reporters on Sunday that new strikes on Iran are ‘highly unlikely’ as long as negotiations keep making progress, and that the United States could hit Iran’s nuclear facilities ‘within five minutes’ if needed. Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Mr. Gharibabadi, said in a televised interview that Tehran is preparing for three scenarios—diplomacy, economic blockade and military aggression—and that from a legal perspective Iran is still in a state of war; he listed Iran’s demands as a permanent end to the war on all fronts, removal of the blockade, resolution of the frozen-assets issue, and lifting of certain sanctions including those on oil. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf said the conflict could end if Washington accepted Iran’s ‘logical conditions’ and warned that if the United States resumes strikes, Iran’s forces would ‘determine the geography of battle.’ Separately, a drone struck the Khor Mor gas field in Iraq’s Sulaymaniyah province on Sunday, setting off a large fire and cutting nearly 2,800 megawatts of regional power generation; no group has claimed it, Kurdish officials called it a terrorist attack, and the Iraqi prime minister’s office ordered a joint investigation with the Kurdish authorities. An Army major who survived the March 1 drone attack on the Port Shuaiba command post in Kuwait, which killed six American soldiers, filed a whistleblower complaint with the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Friday alleging that senior Army officials ignored warnings and failed to plan for anti-drone defences; the Secretary of Defense told a press conference the day after that attack that the troops there were well protected. The President is scheduled to meet Qatar’s prime minister in Washington on Monday, and Qatar has been stepping up efforts to broker an end to the war.

 SubjectiveASEAN NOW — six drones fired at the base in Bahrain, the second attempt in three days after a lull of two monthsIran has launched a drone attack on a United States military base in Bahrain, its second attempt to target the Gulf state in three days, as its stand-off with the United States over the Strait of Hormuz escalates. The Guards said they targeted the American air defence radar facility at the al-Riffa air base using six drones. Bahrain’s military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the attacks before they reached their targets. The attack follows Iranian drones fired at Bahrain on Friday, Tehran’s first attack against Gulf countries since September; the American military said both of Friday’s drones were shot down with no injuries or damage, denying an Iranian claim to have struck an American early warning radar system.

 SubjectiveSalaamedia — four capitals condemn the attack on Bahrain, and Tehran rejects a compensation demandSaudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned Iran’s drone attack on Bahrain on Sunday and expressed solidarity with the kingdom. It was the second attack in three days, after two drones were intercepted at dawn on Friday. Bahrain’s defence forces said their air defence systems intercepted the drones before Iran could achieve its goals, and accused Tehran of a systematic hostile approach. The kingdom issued its first nationwide public safety alert since September, urging residents to move to the nearest safe location. The Guards said they launched six drones at a radar at a United States defence site at the al-Riffa helicopter base, in retaliation for hostile American actions. At his weekly press conference in Tehran on Sunday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Mr. Baghaei, rejected a demand by the Gulf Cooperation Council that Iran pay compensation for its attacks.

 SubjectiveSeatrade Maritime — a tanker attack confirmed by a monitor with the crew safe, and a claimed sinking with no vessel in the footageAn attack on a tanker in the Arabian Gulf has been confirmed while Iran claims two vessels struck mines in Hormuz, including a very large crude carrier which it says sank. The British maritime monitor cited a report from Indian shipping authorities that a tanker was attacked in the Arabian Gulf as it was approaching the Strait of Hormuz on November 15; the crew were reported safe and accounted for, and there were no details of damage. The Guards claimed two tankers struck mines in the southern corridor of the strait, suffering massive explosions during what it described as unauthorised transits, and that a supertanker carrying over 2 million barrels of crude sank in the southern Gulf. The Guards posted video of the supposed sunken tanker on fire; the account records that there is no discernible vessel in the footage, a large fire and smoke billowing on water. The Iranians did not identify either vessel, and there has been no independent verification of the claimed attacks.

 SubjectiveGlobal Insight — the Guards claim a supertanker sunk on a mine, and no independent confirmation has arrivedIran says a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil has sunk in the Persian Gulf after striking a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz. The claim, made by the Revolutionary Guard on Sunday, November 15, is presented in two columns: in the first, the Guard has formally claimed, in a statement carried by state television and reported by Al Arabiya and Gulf News, that two oil tankers travelling along an unauthorised route in the southern part of the strait struck naval mines, resulting in massive explosions and fire, and that one of them—a super tanker carrying over two million barrels of crude—sank in the southern waters of the Gulf. The Guard did not name either vessel, give their flags or owners, or provide casualty figures. In the second column: no independent source has confirmed either incident. The British maritime monitor said the damage and environmental impact were unknown but the crew were safe. The account’s standing rule is printed with it: claims from a party to a conflict need independent corroboration before they can be treated as fact, and that corroboration has not arrived.

 SubjectiveTML — China confirms the Shenzhen meeting on Monday, and the confirmations stand complete from all three sidesChina’s Foreign Ministry confirmed on Monday, November 16, that President Xi Jinping will host a trilateral meeting with President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday, November 19. The session, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, is the first time the three leaders have met together, and Washington says nuclear arms cuts and the Iran war are on its agenda. The White House announced the plan on Friday, November 13, through a communications official, Ms. Wales, and the Kremlin spokesman confirmed on Saturday, November 14, that the three countries had agreed to hold the summit; Beijing, the host, had said only that it was in communication with the relevant parties until Monday’s statement. The meeting takes place on the sidelines of the 33rd APEC Summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, with President Xi chairing the leaders’ meeting of the forum’s 21 member economies. The President is also expected to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with President Xi on November 19, and Washington says there is no plan for a separate meeting between the President and President Putin. A senior American official told the Press the session is meant to begin a conversation on nuclear disarmament, with no agreement expected, and said Ukraine will not be discussed at the three-way session; a Kremlin aide said on November 12 that the Ukraine settlement would be discussed with the President in Shenzhen. The President’s route to the room runs through Manila: he is scheduled to leave Washington on Monday, November 16, attend the ASEAN Summit in the Philippines on November 17, and then travel to Shenzhen for APEC and the trilateral session.

 SubjectiveThe Associated Press, carried by KXL — the President departs Monday, a trade deal with Thailand in Manila, and nuclear talks in ShenzhenPresident Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. His trip begins in Manila and continues to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. In the Philippines, the President will meet Southeast Asian leaders and plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, the White House said. He then heads to China for the APEC summit and, at the end of the trip, the first-ever three-way talks with China’s President Xi and Russia’s President Putin to discuss nuclear stockpiles. The President and American officials have indicated that the meeting will focus on nuclear weapons and that topics of discussion would not include Russia’s war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.

 SubjectiveCNN — the Asia trip as an attempt to reassert authority, and the Huang matter travelling with it to ShenzhenPresident Donald Trump will attempt to reassert his authority this week with a long-planned trip through Asia, punctuated Thursday by an unprecedented three-way meeting with his counterparts from China and Russia. The scandal involving Mr. Huang’s AI chips will loom over the President’s visit to Shenzhen, the hub of China’s tech industry; the President does not intend to raise the spying matter with President Xi, with whom he will meet for the fourth time in just over a year, American officials have previously told the network. At the ASEAN summit in Manila and the APEC summit in Shenzhen he will look to counter the narrative of declining power by announcing new commercial deals and asserting American presence in the region.  SubjectiveStockBiz — the spokesman on force absent an agreement, and Mr. Kushner’s post on expanding the next round to EuropeThe Kremlin spokesperson, Mr. Peskov, said Russia would use force to achieve its goals if it could not reach a security agreement with Europe. In an interview with domestic media on November 15, he said discussions on resolving the Ukraine conflict and establishing a security architecture in Europe would be meaningless without genuine efforts to seek peace. Earlier, speaking to the TASS news agency, he said European negotiators had not yet sought to contact Russia. Trilateral talks between Russia, the United States and Ukraine concluded on November 11 in Abu Dhabi, but no agreements were announced on a ceasefire, territorial disputes or long-term security guarantees. An American envoy, Mr. Kushner, said in a social media post over the weekend that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand participation in the next round of talks to include European partners.

 SubjectiveProfiloPolitics — ‘two component parts, and neither can exist without the other,’ and a channel that waits for a callThe Kremlin warned on Sunday that Russia will achieve its goals in Ukraine by force if Europe leaves no room for negotiation, the spokesman tying any settlement of the war to a new security architecture for the whole continent and saying talks are pointless unless Europe genuinely wants peace. The spokesman’s words to a Vesti correspondent: ‘It is obvious that, one way or another, the settlement in Ukraine will be linked to a new security architecture on the European continent. These are two component parts, and neither can exist without the other.’ He also noted that the negotiators Europe has chosen have not yet attempted to make contact with Russia. The sequence is set out: the trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi ended on Wednesday with no agreement; on Friday, Europe’s leaders agreed to send a five-country team—Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside Union officials—into the process Mr. Kushner is brokering. Europe’s stated position, from the Council President, Mr. Costa, is that ‘only Ukraine has the legitimacy to decide on matters concerning its territory and sovereignty.’ Mr. Kushner announced on Saturday that the focus of the diplomacy is now on bringing Moscow and Europe into direct engagement and on preparing the agenda for the next round of trilateral talks. No date, venue or format for direct Europe-to-Russia talks has been announced. What happens next is a phone call: whether Europe’s team picks up the channel Mr. Kushner has opened, and what Moscow does if it does not.

 SubjectiveValcore News — Ms. Peltola past 50 percent on the dashboard count, her rival waiting for every vote, and counting to WednesdayDemocrat Mary Peltola has claimed victory in Alaska’s Senate race, the only contest of the midterms still without a projected winner. After Saturday’s count she leads Senator Dan Sullivan by more than 11,000 votes and has nudged just past the 50 percent that would spare her a ranked-choice count; Senator Sullivan’s team says it is waiting for every vote, and counting runs to Wednesday, Alaska time. With more than 283,000 ballots counted and write-in votes shared out, Ms. Peltola has 50.1 percent of first-choice votes to Senator Sullivan’s 46.1 percent, a lead of more than 11,000. No winner has been formally projected. Even if she slips back under 50 percent, the ranked-choice tabulation is expected to favour her on the preferences counted so far. A victory would give the Democrats a 56-to-44 Senate majority from January, still short of the 60 votes needed to beat a filibuster. Her campaign declares victory, saying there is no mathematical path for her rival. Senator Sullivan’s spokesman, Mr. Adams, said the campaign was ‘still waiting for every ballot to be counted.’ The Division of Elections will keep counting through Wednesday, the last day it accepts absentee ballots mailed from overseas, followed by ranked-choice tabulation if no one has a majority.

 SubjectiveFish4News — why 49.94 and 50.1 are the same count: the denominator, the 872 write-ins, and 157 votesMs. Peltola remains ahead in Alaska’s unresolved Senate election, with one set of figures placing her just below 50 percent and another displaying slightly more than 50 percent.  SubjectiveKorea JoongAng Daily — Mr. Huang seeks a return four days after resigning, and the petition passes 160,000Days after resigning as Nvidia’s chief, Mr. Huang is reportedly weighing a comeback, with major investors urging the board to consider reinstating him and petitions from employees and shareholders gathering momentum.  SubjectiveUS News Pulse — the letter at 157,000, a shortlist denied, and no word from the boardMr. Huang has discussed a possible return to Nvidia with confidants just four days after resigning as chief executive, a British newspaper reported on Sunday, turning the company’s leadership crisis into a public contest between Silicon Valley, Washington and the board. An open letter calling for his reinstatement passed 157,000 signatures by Sunday, including more than 7,500 self-identified employees of the company, about 18 percent of the workforce. The letter asks the board to reinstate him while an independent investigation establishes the facts. Investors Mr. Gerstner and Mr. Baker wrote to the board on Friday urging it to keep a return among the options. The Treasury Secretary said on Sunday that the company’s leadership needs a dramatic overhaul and pressed for an outsider. The board denied reports it had shortlisted the chief of Arm, Mr. Haas. The board has not commented publicly, and the company declined to confirm the newspaper’s report. No return has been announced; Mr. Huang has not said publicly that he wants the job back, and Ms. Kress remains interim chief executive. The company reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, November 17, five days after Mr. Huang resigned.

### Sunday Closes at More Than 2,300 Flights Cancelled With the Root Cause Still Unknown, Washington Files Its First Word on the Bahrain Radar — No Impacts to American Forces, With the Radar Itself Unaddressed — and Nvidia's Contest Turns Open, a War Room for Mr. Huang Against a Treasury Call for an Outside Successor

Filed as: Edition No. 53 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-16T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-16-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Sunday Closes at More Than 2,300 Flights Cancelled With the Root Cause Still Unknown, Washington Files Its First Word on the Bahrain Radar—No Impacts to American Forces, With the Radar Itself Unaddressed—and Nvidia’s Contest Turns Open, a War Room for Mr. Huang Against a Treasury Call for an Outside Successor

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a third day of disruption that closed larger than its early count and smaller than Saturday, with its cause narrowed to two routers and its root cause still unnamed; a radar claim that gained one narrow American sentence and no assessment of the radar; a count that spent Sunday unmoved; and a company whose succession stopped being a board matter and became an open contest, six days of it now dated by other men’s deadlines.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Monday, November 16, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 52, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Sunday, in Edition No. 50, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Sunday, in Edition No. 49, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Sunday, and in Edition No. 48, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Sunday. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Sunday Settled, What It Left Open

Sunday settled the size of its own disruption at more than 2,300 flights cancelled and some 7,700 delayed, settled that Washington will speak about Bahrain in one narrow sentence and no wider, and settled that Nvidia’s succession is now contested in public from two directions at once; it left open the root cause of Friday’s stop, the condition of the radar at Al-Riffa, the call in Alaska, and the board’s answer to everyone. The final flight count stands in the final wire account filed below, against more than 1,600 cancelled in the day’s early count in the early wire account filed below; the same final account carries the second router, at Amarillo, Texas, the disabling of some 60 similar routers, and the Secretary’s sentence that the root cause is not known. The American sentence on Bahrain stands in the radar account filed below: a Central Command spokesman told a newspaper there were no impacts to American forces, and the statement did not say whether radar equipment was damaged. Alaska’s count stands where Saturday left it, at 140,637 to 129,424 in the state’s report filed below, uncalled, with the next count due Monday. Nvidia’s two directions stand in the contest account filed below and in the petition account filed below. Monday carries the first tests of the new week: the airlines read against the Secretary’s fully-normal promise, the President’s departure for Asia, Alaska’s next count, and a central bank chairman’s noon remarks. The desk takes the files in that order.

The Airlines at Midnight: More Than 2,300 Cancelled at the Close, a Second Router at Amarillo, and No Root Cause

The day’s last count is larger than the day’s early count, and the desk prints both, at their hours. More than 2,300 flights were cancelled and some 7,700 delayed on Sunday, with more than 10,000 flights affected, in the final wire account above; the early wire account counted more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 3,600 delayed, and the tracker account counted nearly 1,700 cancelled by 1350, in the accounts filed below. The final shares are heavier than the early ones: 28 percent of JetBlue’s Sunday flights cancelled, against 27 percent earlier, and 17 percent of American’s, against 13 percent earlier, with United, Southwest and Delta at 3 to 5 percent in both counts, in the final account. Saturday stands at more than 6,400 cancelled and more than 8,000 delayed in the same account, and Friday’s stop, which halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours, stands as the longest nationwide halt since September 11, 2001, in the same account. No second stop was ordered on Sunday. Monday’s cancellations stood at 33 on Sunday afternoon in the tracker account, and no later Monday figure stands in the midnight file; Monday will be read, as the evening edition put it, against the Secretary’s promise of a system probably fully normal on Monday, and against the Administrator’s earlier promise of full schedule integrity by Sunday’s close, which Sunday’s final count did not meet.

The cause file gained a second town, a disabled fleet of routers, and an admission. The replacement of a router at El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered problems with a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other centers, the Secretary said on a Sunday programme, in the final wire account above; the functionality of the originating routers has been disabled, and the Administration did the same for about 60 similar routers in the system, in the same account. The routers that experienced issues were purchased in 2001 and were obsolete by 2006, in the same account. On the man who installed the first router, the Secretary said he was a good American patriot and a veteran, that sabotage is not believed, and that there is no evidence of a cyberattack or other malicious intent—and then the admission that closes the file for the night: the Administration still does not know what ultimately caused a problem in maintenance work done thousands of times before without issue, and does not actually have the root cause, in the same account. The money file moved on Sunday in three voices: the President made his first public comments on the weekend’s disruption, calling for the $50 billion upgrade to be approved and done all at once, not in drips and drabs, in the same account; the Secretary’s request stands at $50 billion, up from $30 billion, after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year, in the same account; and two House members answered on Saturday that about $11 billion of that $12.5 billion remains unspent and asked why more is needed, in the same account, against the Secretary’s Sunday answer that last year’s money was earmarked for certain spending and did not include new software. Settled: Sunday’s cost, the two routers, and the absence of any sign of attack. Open: the root cause, in the Secretary’s own words.

Bahrain at Midnight: One Narrow American Sentence, No Word on the Radar, and Article 51 Claimed Both Ways

Washington’s silence, which the evening edition recorded as a fact of the file, ended before midnight—narrowly. A Central Command spokesman, Mr. Hawkins, told a newspaper that there were no impacts to American forces, in the radar account above; the statement did not say whether radar equipment or other property was damaged, and Manama had not answered the newspaper’s question about damage at the site, in the same account. That is the whole of the American word on Sunday’s claim at 0000: it answers for the men and not for the machine, and the desk prints it at exactly that width. The two claims it stands between are unchanged. The Guards say six drones of their Aerospace Force targeted the American air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base, in a second phase of retaliation, in the Bahrain account filed below; the Defence Force says its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, in the same account; and no damage and no casualties have been reported in any account in the file.

The written file around the claim is complete, and it is aligned on one side and answered on the other. Manama’s Foreign Ministry statement stands whole in the ministry account filed below: the strongest condemnation, Iran held fully responsible, the transformation of Bahraini territory into an arena for settling scores rejected, Security Council Resolution 2817 cited, and Bahrain’s right of self-defence under Article 51 affirmed, with a call on the Security Council, where Bahrain sits, to condemn the attacks and take decisive measures. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the attacks and stood with Manama, in the condemnations account filed below, which carries their four sentences severally: a violation of international law and good neighbourliness from Riyadh, a flagrant violation of sovereignty from Doha, a threat to security and territorial integrity from Amman, and a dangerous escalation from Cairo. Tehran’s spokesman, Mr. Baghaei, defended the strikes as justified in self-defence and said Iran would keep responding to military aggression, in the evening file, and rejected a Cooperation Council demand that Iran pay compensation for its attacks, in the condemnations account above. Article 51 therefore stands claimed in the same file by Manama for its defence and by Tehran for its strikes. The President’s Saturday condition, that he might hold off on attacking Iran if there were no new provocations, stands unapplied to Sunday’s claim in any statement in the midnight file. Settled: the responses, all of them, in writing. Open: what, if anything, was hit at Al-Riffa.

The Count at Midnight: No Sunday Count, 157 Short of a Majority, and Monday as the Next Fact

Alaska’s Senate count spent Sunday exactly where Saturday afternoon left it, and midnight adds nothing to it but the calendar. The state’s unofficial summary, timed 1515 on Saturday, gives Ms. Peltola 140,637 votes, 49.94 percent; Senator Sullivan 129,424, 45.96 percent; Mr. Heikes 6,002; Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,652; and write-ins 872, on 281,587 votes in the race, with all 401 precincts reported, in the state’s report above. The lead is 11,213 votes. A majority of the reported vote is 140,794, and Ms. Peltola stands 157 votes short of it by the desk’s arithmetic; the state’s dashboard, which excludes unresolved write-ins from its display calculation, rounds her share to 50.1 percent, in the lead account filed below, which also records that the latest batch added 2,397 votes for Ms. Peltola and 1,596 for Senator Sullivan. The Press estimates 97 percent counted and has not called the race; one tracker lists a winner; Ms. Peltola declared victory on Saturday; the President declared Senator Sullivan the winner on November 7; and Senator Sullivan has not conceded, in the lead account and in the majority account filed below, which records her campaign’s position that Senator Sullivan has no mathematical path. The next count is due Monday. Overseas ballots may arrive through Wednesday, November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled if no candidate holds a majority; certification is targeted for November 25. Settled at midnight: nothing new, and the desk says so plainly—a day without a count is a fact of a count that has run twelve days. Open: the call, the tabulation, and 157 votes.

Shenzhen and Europe at Midnight: A Departure on Monday, Two Confirmations and a Silence, and Two Sentences From Moscow

The President departs Monday for Manila and the ASEAN meetings and continues to Shenzhen, due there November 17 through 19, and that departure is the next fact in the week’s largest file. The meeting of the three presidents on Thursday, November 19, stands confirmed by the White House on Friday and by the Kremlin on Saturday, and unconfirmed by its host, in the agenda account filed below and in the meeting account filed below; China’s Friday sentence, that it is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state, stands unamended at midnight. The agenda split stands whole: nuclear arms and Iran in the American telling, with no agreement expected in the same telling, and Ukraine off the trilateral agenda in the American telling and on it in the Kremlin aide’s. No third confirmation came on Sunday, and no agenda was agreed in any account in the midnight file.

Europe’s file closed Sunday as it opened, with one spokesman’s two answers carried by the wires and no European answer to either. Asked by the TASS agency whether Europe’s negotiators have attempted to contact Russia, spokesman Peskov answered, “No, not yet,” in the contact account filed below; in an interview with a Vesti correspondent he said that in the absence of a negotiated solution Russia will have to achieve its objectives by force, and that if the Union does not want peace there is no point in discussing a settlement or a European security framework, in the force account filed below. The standing American sentence, that the delegation at Abu Dhabi ensured Europe will be included in future talks, stands where the week left it. No date for a first contact stands in the file, and no next round of the trilateral talks carries a date or a place at midnight.

Nvidia at Midnight: A War Room on One Side, a Treasury Deadline on the Other, and No Answer From the Board

Sunday turned a board matter into an open contest, and both sides of it are now on the record. Mr. Huang has discussed a return with confidants, and allies are assembling a war room of Silicon Valley executives to lobby the board and to seek support from the White House, in the contest account above and in the comeback account filed below. The petition’s counter stood at 154,678 names at 1001 Pacific on Sunday, with 7,459 self-described current employees, 1,406 former employees, 81,896 shareholders and 63,917 other supporters, its affiliations self-reported and its fake entries named in its own accounts, in the petition account above; a later account put the counter at 156,850. The petition’s asks stand in the campaign account filed below: reinstatement while an independent investigation establishes the facts, the investigation’s scope and timetable made public, a substantive opportunity to respond, and, if the board insists he leave, a specific, evidence-backed explanation. The Gerstner and Baker letter asks for a slow and deliberate search that keeps Mr. Huang’s return among the options, in the contest account.

The other side of the contest spoke on a Sunday programme, and it spoke in deadlines. The Treasury Secretary, Mr. Bessent, said on a Sunday programme that the board needs to look outside the company and that Nvidia needs sweeping change in its leadership, in the contest account above; he questioned whether the company knowingly violated export controls on high-end chips, pointed to sales billed through Singapore and to the company’s having stopped disclosing Singapore revenue separately, and said answers are needed from the board and from external counsel within 10 days, in the same account. A House committee chairman said on Sunday that Mr. Huang has agreed to appear for closed-door testimony before three House committees, in the same account. On succession, the board has contacted the chief of Arm as a potential successor and states that no formal process has yet been initiated, in the same account. The board itself had filed no public answer by midnight—not to the petition, not to the Gerstner and Baker letter, and not to the Treasury Secretary—in any account the desk read. No finding has been made by the board, by any committee or by any court on any allegation in this file. Earnings stand on Tuesday, November 17, after the close, with consensus revenue at $108.9 billion against the company’s outlook of $108.0 billion in the week’s file, and the interim chief, Ms. Kress, leads the call. Settled: the contest, its two directions, and its 10-day clock. Open: the board’s first word.

The Markets at Midnight: Futures Open Higher at 1800, Stand Lower by 2036, and Bitcoin Holds Above $65,000

The week’s first market fact is a rise that did not hold. Futures opened higher on Sunday evening: at 1810 Eastern the S&P 500 futures were up 0.2 percent at about 7,600 and the Nasdaq 100 futures up 0.6 percent, with Dow futures little changed and crude slightly lower, in the futures account filed below. By 2036 Eastern the same three contracts stood lower: Dow futures down 0.11 percent, S&P 500 futures down 0.22 percent and Nasdaq-100 futures down 0.58 percent, in the late futures account filed below, which puts Brent at $95.33, down about 0.53 percent, and West Texas crude at $88.26, down 0.34 percent. Friday’s closes stand beneath both readings: the S&P 500 at 7,561.67, down 0.40 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 25,136.27, down 0.91; the Dow at 52,347.60, up 0.10; and the ten-year yield at 5.15 percent. Bitcoin stood near $65,200 on Sunday evening, down about 5 percent since Friday’s close, after touching about $62,000 on Saturday, its lowest since July, in the futures account above; the day’s other readings, from $61,946 to $65,714, stand in the evening file. The week’s market calendar is dated in every account: the central bank chairman speaks Monday at noon, retail sales and Nvidia come Tuesday, the October meeting minutes come Wednesday, and Thursday carries a retailer’s earnings, a listing, and Shenzhen.

France and Spain at Midnight: A Senate Date on Thursday in Paris, and a New Tracking in Spain

France’s fifth Saturday stands closed at the numbers the evening edition printed, and its next facts are weekday facts. The Interior Ministry’s count stands at 106,000 nationwide, 24,000 in Paris, down from 146,000 the Saturday before, with 219 detained in the week’s file; the organisers’ count stands at about 200,000, in the demonstrations account filed below, which records demands from protecting children and increasing wages to more resources for education and protest against the police bill. That bill, giving officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when they use firearms and called a licence to kill by its critics in the accounts, is scheduled to be examined by the Senate on Thursday, November 19, in the Senate account filed below. The unions’ Tuesday strike stands, called after the government’s 0.6 percent minimum-wage promise was rejected; Tuesday is also the eighth anniversary of the Yellow Vest movement, and a sixth Saturday is called for November 21.

Spain’s campaign stands where Sunday’s new tracking left it. The first instalment of a new tracking puts the Popular Party at 30.8 percent and 130 seats, the Socialists at 26.4 percent and 106 seats, and Vox at 18.2 percent and 65 seats, a combined 195 seats for the first and third parties against 176 needed for a majority, in the tracking account filed below. The mean of sixteen institutes stands at Popular Party 31.4, Socialists 26.9 and Vox 19.1, in the evening file; the state survey’s Socialist lead stands against both figures where the week left it. A head-to-head television debate is reported set for November 19, and polls may publish until November 23. Spain votes on November 29.

Monday at Midnight: Every File in This Edition Is Dated, and Monday Holds Four of the Dates

Monday carries the recovery’s verdict, the President’s departure, Alaska’s next count, and the central bank chairman’s remarks at noon. The airlines will be read against the Secretary’s fully-normal promise and against Sunday’s final count of more than 2,300 cancelled. Alaska’s count resumes ahead of Wednesday’s tabulation. Tuesday carries retail sales, France’s strike, and Nvidia’s earnings after the close. Wednesday carries the October meeting minutes, the APEC leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, and Alaska’s tabulation. Thursday carries the three presidents in Shenzhen, the Senate’s examination of the police bill in Paris, and a listing in New York. The Treasury Secretary’s 10 days run from Sunday. Spain votes November 29; Mr. Huang’s interview stands dated December 1; the Federal Reserve decides December 8 and 9. The Overnight Watch collects at 0400.

The Cocked Hat

Where the midnight’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Sunday’s cost: more than 2,300 cancelled and some 7,700 delayed in the final wire count, more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 3,600 delayed in the early wire count, nearly 1,700 cancelled by 1350 in the tracker account, and 1,606 cancelled at 1100 in the El Dorado account—readings taken at different hours, agreeing on the day’s order and on nothing finer; and on its shares, American at 17 percent in the final count against 13 percent in the early one, JetBlue at 28 against 27. On the promise: full schedule integrity by Sunday’s close in the Administrator’s Saturday words, probably fully normal on Monday in the Secretary’s Sunday words, and a final Sunday count that met neither in full. On the failed thing: a router at El Dorado triggering a second router at Amarillo and a flood across the centers, some 60 similar routers disabled, equipment purchased in 2001 and obsolete by 2006, and the root cause unknown in the Secretary’s own admission. On Bahrain: intercepts and destruction in the Defence Force’s account, six drones on target in the Guards’, condemnations from four neighbouring capitals, Article 51 claimed by both sides, no impacts to American forces in the Central Command spokesman’s sentence, and no word from any capital on the condition of the radar itself. On Alaska’s share: 49.94 percent on the state’s full denominator, 50.1 on the dashboard that excludes unresolved write-ins, a winner listed on one tracker, no call from the Press, a victory declared by one candidate and a winner declared by the President for the other, and no count at all on Sunday. On Europe: not yet contacted in the spokesman’s answer, included in future talks in the White House’s November 13 sentence, and objectives by force absent a negotiated solution in the spokesman’s interview, with no European answer in the file. On Shenzhen: confirmed by Washington and Moscow, unconfirmed by its host, with Ukraine on the agenda in one capital’s telling and off it in another’s. On Nvidia: a war room and a counter at 154,678 and 156,850 in two Sunday readings on one side, a call for an outside successor and answers within 10 days from the Treasury on the other, and no answer from the board to either. On futures: up 0.2 and 0.6 percent at the 1800 open, down 0.22 and 0.58 percent by 2036. On France: 106,000 in the Ministry’s count and about 200,000 in the organisers’. On Spain: 30.8 percent for the Popular Party in the new tracking, 31.4 in the sixteen-institute mean, and a Socialist lead in the state survey. Inside the triangle is where the day honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 26 items.

 

 SubjectiveReuters via BusinessWorld — more than 2,300 cancelled and some 7,700 delayed on Sunday at the final count, a second router at Amarillo, and no root causeUnited States air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but the Transportation Secretary predicted a return to normalcy by Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop. More than 2,300 flights nationwide were canceled and some 7,700 were delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware; airlines on Saturday had canceled more than 6,400 flights and delayed more than 8,000. The Secretary said on a Sunday programme that there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other malicious intent, but the cause remained unclear, and that flights would come back to normal on Sunday but probably fully normal on Monday. On Sunday 28 percent of JetBlue flights and 17 percent of American Airlines flights were canceled, with United, Southwest and Delta reporting cancellations of 3 to 5 percent. The replacement of a router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered problems with a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other centers; the functionality of the originating routers has been disabled, as was done for about 60 similar routers. The routers were purchased in 2001 and were obsolete by 2006. The Secretary said the worker who installed the router was a good American patriot and a veteran, that sabotage is not believed, and that the Administration does not actually have the root cause. The President made his first public comments on the weekend’s disruption, calling for additional funding to be approved and done all at once; two House members answered that about $11 billion of the $12.5 billion approved last year remains unspent.

 SubjectiveReuters via Virginia Business — more than 1,600 cancelled and almost 3,600 delayed on Sunday in the early count, and a return to normalcy predicted by MondayUnited States air travel disruptions continued for a third day on Sunday with more than 5,200 flights already affected, but the Transportation Secretary predicted a return to normalcy by Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule after a systemwide ground stop. More than 1,600 flights nationwide were cancelled and almost 3,600 were delayed on Sunday, according to FlightAware; airlines on Saturday had cancelled more than 6,400 flights and delayed more than 8,000. The Secretary said flights will come back to normal on Sunday but probably fully normal on Monday, and emphasised the Administration’s focus on keeping passengers safe. On Sunday 27 percent of JetBlue flights and 13 percent of American Airlines flights were cancelled, with Southwest, United and Delta reporting cancellations of 3 to 5 percent of their flights. The Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours.

 SubjectiveThe Points Guy — nearly 1,700 cancelled by 1350 Sunday, more than 17,000 scrubbed since Friday, and 33 of Monday’s downSunday was shaping up to be another rough day at airports across the country, with travellers facing a third straight day of widespread cancellations after Friday’s nationwide ground stop. As of 1:50 p.m. Eastern on Sunday, nearly 1,700 flights had been cancelled and another 5,280 had been delayed, according to FlightAware; all told, more than 17,000 flights have been scrubbed since Friday. Cancellations appeared to slow entering Sunday compared with the past two days, but operations had not returned to normal, especially on some carriers. The Administrator had said disruptions were expected to begin easing by Sunday evening, and that the airline partners believe they will be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday. As of Sunday afternoon, 33 flights for Monday had been cancelled, a total that had not increased much since the morning, suggesting operations may be stabilising. The account records the ground stop’s cause as a communications outage affecting air traffic control discovered late Friday afternoon.

 SubjectiveSourceFirst News — the El Dorado, Arkansas router, 1,606 cancelled by 1100, and a full return that could slip into MondayFriday’s nationwide ground stop began when a newly installed router at a remote Administration site in El Dorado, Arkansas, started flooding the air traffic control network, the Transportation Secretary said on Sunday; officials still do not know whether the fault lay with the equipment or with the contractor that installed it. Both routers are now with L3Harris, the contractor that owns and operates the network, while Administration staff are on site and the Federal Bureau of Investigation is offering support. As investigators examine the Arkansas router, FlightAware counted 1,606 United States flight cancellations by 11 a.m. Eastern on Sunday, against 6,696 for all of Saturday, and 3,343 delayed. The Administration’s airport status feed showed no ground stop anywhere at 11 a.m. The Administrator had promised on Saturday that schedules would be back to normal by the close of business Sunday; on Sunday the Secretary moved that toward Monday, saying planes and crews were still out of position.

 SubjectiveFana News — Bahrain strongly condemns Iran’s continued attacks, citing Resolution 2817 and Article 51Bahrain has condemned, in the strongest terms, Iran’s continued attacks on its territory after air defence systems intercepted and destroyed drones launched on Sunday, two days after intercepting two others in a similar attack. The Foreign Ministry described the attacks as a resumption of Iran’s aggression against Bahrain and regional countries, in blatant disregard for international law and the Charter; a flagrant violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and neighbouring countries and demanded their immediate cessation; and a foreclosing of de-escalation efforts imperilling regional security and stability. The ministry affirmed Bahrain’s inherent individual and collective right to self-defence under Article 51 and to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents. As a member of the Security Council, Bahrain called on the Council to condemn the repeated attacks, shoulder its responsibilities, and take decisive measures to ensure Iran’s full compliance with Resolution 2817.

 SubjectiveSalaamedia — Arab states condemn Iran’s drone attack on Bahrain, and Tehran rejects a compensation demandSaudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned Iran’s drone attack on Bahrain on Sunday and expressed solidarity with the kingdom. The Guards said they launched six drones at a radar at a United States defence site at the al-Riffa helicopter base, in retaliation for hostile United States actions. In Riyadh, the Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks in the strongest terms, saying they violated international law and the principles of good neighbourliness. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said the continued attacks were a flagrant violation of Bahrain’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a breach of international law and the Charter. Jordan’s Foreign Ministry said the attacks violated Bahrain’s sovereignty and threatened its security, stability and territorial integrity. In Cairo, the Foreign Ministry said the attacks were a dangerous escalation that violated Bahrain’s sovereignty and threatened its security.  SubjectiveKhabarWire — Iran strikes a Bahrain air base for a second time in days, and the Gulf closes ranksThe Guards said they launched six drones at an American air-defence radar at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain before dawn on Sunday, the second attack on the kingdom in three days; Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they reached their targets, and the Interior Ministry issued two public alerts telling residents to seek shelter. Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry expressed the kingdom’s strongest condemnation, described the attack as a violation of Resolution 2817, said no pretext could justify aggression against a state’s sovereignty, rejected the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores, held Iran responsible, and invoked Article 51 and the Cooperation Council’s joint defence agreement.
